lessons.title: What organic buyers want
lessons.html:
The organic market

Some people want to buy food that is grown without synthetic chemical fertilisers and sprays. This food is called organic. Organic buyers are often willing to pay more. You may find organic products in supermarkets, at farmers' markets, in health shops, in restaurants, and in boxes delivered to homes. Some organic products, like rooibos tea, are exported to other countries.

What makes a product organic

  • No synthetic chemical fertilisers. Use compost, manure and green manure crops instead.
  • No synthetic chemical sprays for pests and weeds. Use natural methods such as crop rotation, hand weeding, mulching and helpful insects. Only some approved natural products may be used.
  • No genetically modified (GM) seed.
  • For animals: good living conditions, organic feed, and no routine use of growth promoters.

Buyers need proof

A buyer cannot see if a tomato is organic by looking at it. So most buyers, especially shops and exporters, want proof:

  • A certificate from a certification body that has inspected the farm.
  • Or, for local sales, membership of a Participatory Guarantee System (PGS), where farmers and buyers check each other's farms.

A farm cannot just say its product is organic. Using the word organic on a label without proof can mislead buyers and lose their trust.

Quality is still important

Organic buyers also want good quality. Organic produce must be fresh, clean, the right size and ripeness, and free of damage and rot, just like other produce. Being organic does not mean poor-looking produce is accepted.

lessons.title: Meeting the requirements every day
lessons.html:
What you must do on an organic farm

Use only allowed inputs

  • Use only the compost, manure, seed and sprays your supervisor gives you for the organic fields.
  • Never bring in a fertiliser or spray from the store for another farm or block without asking.
  • If you are not sure if something is allowed, ask before you use it.

Keep organic and non-organic apart

Some farms grow both organic and normal crops. They must never get mixed.

  • Use clean crates, bags and tools marked for organic produce.
  • Do not put organic produce on a bakkie or in a store where chemicals are kept.
  • Keep organic produce on separate shelves or in a separate area.
  • Clean machines before they move from a normal field to an organic field.

Protect the organic fields

  • Keep the buffer strip between organic fields and neighbours' fields. It stops spray drift.
  • Tell your supervisor if you see a neighbour spraying near the organic fields.

Keep records

Inspectors check records. Help keep them correct:

  • What was planted, where and when.
  • What compost or other inputs were used, how much and when.
  • What was harvested, from which field, and how much.
  • Where it was sent.

Packing and labelling

  • Pack in clean containers.
  • Labels must show the correct product and that it is organic, only if the farm is certified.
  • Label each crate with the field or batch so it can be traced.

Hygiene

Wash your hands before handling produce, use clean toilets and never handle food when you are sick with a stomach problem. Buyers check food safety too.

Key points

  • Organic food is grown without synthetic fertilisers, synthetic sprays or GM seed.
  • Buyers need proof, such as a certificate or PGS membership.
  • Organic produce must still be of good quality.
  • Use only allowed inputs and keep organic produce separate.
  • Keep records and label crates so produce can be traced.
